vignette:
Omar, at fifty-four, carried himself with a quiet dignity that belied the constant storm within. A community organizer known for his steady presence, he now found it nearly impossible to be present at all. The man who once thrived on connecting with people now spent his days trying to become invisible. The shift began eighteen months ago, on a night that shattered his life into pieces that no longer fit together. He had been with his partner for five years, building a life he trusted. That trust was annihilated in the darkness of their shared bedroom. The argument, like others before, had escalated, but this time it broke through a final, terrifying barrier. The last thing he remembered clearly before the assault began was the rhythmic, chopping sound of a news helicopter hovering somewhere over their neighborhood, its blades beating a soundtrack to his terror.

In the weeks and months that followed, the event refused to remain in the past. It lived in him, not as a coherent story, but as a series of jagged, sensory fragments. Sometimes, without any warning, the sound of a distant aircraft would flood his senses, and he would be back in that room, his heart hammering against his ribs. He would hear the helicopter blades in his head, a phantom auditory echo that was as real as any sound in the present moment. Other times, it would be a flash of the overturned bedside lamp, or the specific pattern of the plaster on the ceiling. These disconnected pieces would ambush him, leaving him disoriented and breathless. He came to believe the attack wasn't just a random, awful event, but a direct consequence of some fundamental flaw within him. The event happened, he was certain, because of the sort of person he was—too trusting, too soft, too weak. This self-blame was a constant, corrosive whisper in his mind.

This new, terrifying understanding of himself and the world reshaped his entire existence. His fundamental belief that people were basically good and that he was safe had been utterly destroyed. Now, the world was a landscape of hidden threats. As a community organizer, his job required him to be in meeting halls, church basements, and public parks—places now fraught with peril. During neighborhood council meetings, instead of focusing on zoning issues, he would find himself scanning the faces in the crowd, assessing each person for potential danger, his body coiled and ready to flee. He started wearing hoodies and baseball caps, even indoors, keeping his head down in an effort to deflect attention. He felt a desperate need to conceal himself, to move through the world without being noticed.

His daily commute became a complex series of detours. The apartment where the assault occurred was in a neighborhood he now avoided with meticulous care, even if it meant adding an hour to his travel time. Just seeing the familiar street signs or the corner bodega was enough to trigger a cascade of memories and a suffocating wave of panic. This avoidance extended beyond physical locations. He had become a ghost in his own life, his vibrant energy replaced by a drained, watchful stillness. His wife, Layla, noticed him growing more distant, his explanations for his strange routines becoming less and less convincing. The betrayal he felt from his ex-partner had poisoned his ability to trust anyone, even the woman he loved.

He finally sought therapy after an incident last month. While walking with Layla in a park, a police helicopter flew low overhead. Omar froze, his eyes wide with a terror she could not understand. He was gone, his mind trapped in that dark room from long ago, the present moment completely erased. It took several minutes for her voice to pull him back. Seeing the fear and confusion in her eyes, he realized he could not keep the pieces of his shattered life hidden any longer. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but a small part of him hopes he can one day walk outside on a clear night, hear a helicopter pass overhead, and feel nothing but the cool air on his skin.
